articles.preview: Accusations of incompetence follow retreat of Riyadh-backed forces in effort to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

Many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

The Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.

The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.

The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.

The retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.

He said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

“The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”

The breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh said reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

He also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter said. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

The former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking said the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed’s victory is a blow to the politics of Islamophobia
articles.summary: He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward.
articles.preview: He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward. The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congressional majorities and brought Democrats back into the spotlight was called everything from a flood to a political earthquake. In a montage on The Daily Show, TV anchors reduced the night to a gleeful succession of words and phrases like “rout” and “shellacking”.
articles.body:
He embraced his Muslim identity, put Gaza on the ballot and showed Democrats a different way forward.

The blue wave that swept Republicans from their congressional majorities and brought Democrats back into the spotlight was called everything from a flood to a political earthquake. In a montage on The Daily Show, TV anchors reduced the night to a gleeful succession of words and phrases like “rout” and “shellacking”. On Zeteo’s election-night coverage with Mehdi Hasan, Prem Thakker coined the term “Tsunamanani”, a brief injection of comic irony amid serious news and analysis. The night was all those things.

Arguably the most significant victory of the congressional sweep was Abdul El-Sayed’s win over Trump-backed extremist Mike Rogers, whose candidacy was propped up by roughly $169 million in outside spending benefiting him, including spending by Republican super PACs tied to Donald Trump and Elon Musk. El-Sayed will be the first Muslim ever to grace the floor of the US Senate.

It was hard to look away from the joy on El-Sayed’s face as he shared the win. His words were just as striking, offering a vision of how American politics could be redirected towards peace and humanity. He told the crowd:“Michiganders, we want our taxes spent here, for schools here and healthcare here, and infrastructure here. We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid or genocide or war.”

When he said, “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honored to stand here as your senator elect,” the crowd roared. Throughout the campaign, right-wing enthusiasts had used his whole name to brand him a “terrorist”, a “jihadist” and “a danger to the American public”. By pronouncing that name, complete with its Arabic intonation, he reclaimed what pundits and politicians, including Donald Trump, had spent months mocking. Later in the speech, El-Sayed joked, “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name, so after JD swears me in in January, you could just go on and call me Senator.” The crowd roared again.

He also said, “You might have noticed, I always say Inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that Inshallah into a…”

One minute and twenty seconds into his speech, the crowd shouted the answer together: “Alhamdulillah!” Then the hall filled with chants of “Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul! Abdul!”

Still smiling, El-Sayed added, “For the right-wing ops, that just means praise be to God.”

When we heard the thunderous applause for his name and for “Alhamdulillah”, one of the most common yet sacred expressions in Islam, it felt as though a deeply entrenched stereotype about Islam and Muslims was being shattered, undermining the Islamophobia that has been used to stir fear and hatred in American politics.

With no meaningful policy accomplishments to point to and a wildly unpopular Donald Trump, Republicans resorted to a relentlessly bigoted smear campaign against El-Sayed.

The attacks he faced were part of a broader pattern of organised anti-Muslim prejudice, extending beyond bots and social media influencers into Republican politics and policymaking. As documented by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, this hostility was being promoted through social media, legislation and a congressional caucus. According to the CSOH, 89 Republican elected officials took part in a coordinated anti-Muslim campaign over thirteen months: 46 of them published 1,111 social media posts, eight Sharia-related bills were introduced, and the Sharia-Free America Caucus grew to 62 members by April 2026.

Political advisers told El-Sayed that “someone with a name and my story, a Muslim, was unelectable”, as if anti-Muslim prejudice were an immovable grassroots bias. In reality, it was a prejudice deliberately cultivated and promoted with millions of dollars from billionaire funders, most of them Zionists.

When he entered the race for the US Senate, El-Sayed accepted the challenge of confronting the toxic Islamophobia built on the othering of Muslims and Islam. He refused to be demonised or to accept the artificial divide between “us” and “them”, responding with skilful verbal panache, always in his own words. At his final campaign rally, his wife, Dr Sarah Jukaku, introduced him with the words, “With Abdul, what you see is what you get … No corporation, no billionaire, no special interest. No one tells him what to do or what to say.” He offered voters an alternative, one notably humanistic and built on the promise of diversity, unity and a community of care. He put Gaza on the ballot as part of his vision.

Abdul El-Sayed is an American, a Midwesterner, a doctor and a husband who talks to his mother on a swing and pops up behind his grandparents on a video tape as a way to affirm his midwestern values. He worked in public health to help provide glasses to 16,000 children from low-income families in Detroit and Wayne County.

He is also a Muslim man with a long Middle Eastern name who speaks Arabic. As an American and a Muslim, he lays bare the lies that have dehumanised Muslims for so long. He visits farmers and residents across Michigan, including rural conservatives in the Upper Peninsula. When media pundits present his religion as a threat to Americans, he doesn’t back down. He talks openly about Islam and his identity, rejecting the narrow mindset of those who would brand him “foreign”. He places his religion in the context of Judaism and Christianity. In one video filmed at a Rosh Hashanah dinner, he talks with his Jewish hostesses, who recite a prayer before they share home-cooked kugel.

He invented new ways to talk about religion. In one campaign ad, he looks into the camera and says he prays, and that we all “need faith and hope that we can fix things”. The ad ends with, “I’m Abdul El-Sayed, a man of faith. That’s a good thing.”

In his speech on election night, he returned to the connection between war and the economy, which helps explain the blowback that cost Republicans control of Congress. He said, “It just shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or fill your tank. It shouldn’t be this hard to see a doctor in the richest, most powerful country in the world. It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money’s going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.” His words bring together the suffering of those caught in wars funded by our tax dollars and those deprived of their basic needs at home.

He used his voice to broaden the horizons of American politics, offering a vision that could reshape how we imagine America: a more expansive country where we all fit, embracing its diversity and rejecting the violence, hate and exclusion of the shrinking Trumpian world. He closed his speech with the call, “We deserve an America for all her kids. So Michigan, let’s go build it.”

Abdul El-Sayed’s accomplishment was a major blow to a world built on Arab and Muslim hate. He embodies, by contrast, a politics of joy, care, concern, justice and equality, and the possibility of an America so often lost to our imaginations in a world at war.

Now the so-called “centrist” or “moderate” Democrats must decide whether to champion a new anti-Islamophobic politics or keep taking money from hate mongers and mass murderers, and face the consequences of the same political blowback that cost Republicans their majorities.

A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.body:
A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.

Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”

The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.

The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.

“We’ve got to start with a broad document, concentrate on getting agreement with some difficult issues, then refine it down over the coming days,” Bowen told the Guardian in an interview.

Alden Mayer, a senior associate at the E3G thinktank, said putting out the draft text at this stage was a gamble. “But it would also be a gamble to wait until later in the week. They have decided to take the ‘full monty’ approach, knowing that many of the 144 paragraphs will not survive the week,” he said. “The question is where does the presidency think the sweet spot is on the various contested issues.”

The wording on fossil fuels echoes a pledge made by all countries at Cop28 in Dubai to “transition away from fossil fuels”, which had no timetable or work programme attached, but is likely to be attacked by oil-producing countries that have hardened their positions since then.

There are also provisions to address the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris agreement and a target to derive 35% of global final energy from electricity by 2035, a key priority for the host nation, Turkey.

Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, called the text “an overgrown garden. There are lots of encouraging green shoots but there are also a lot of weeds that need to be pulled out.”

He welcomed the fleshing out in the draft of a previous promise to triple finance to poor countries to help them adapt to the impacts of extreme weather. “If that language remains in the final version, it would suggest countries are starting to listen to the needs of the vulnerable,” he said.

The “cover decision” is one part of the expected outcome of this Cop, and some countries – chiefly Russia, Saudi Arabia and the Arab group and some allies – have objected to having one. Cover decisions have been used in most of the 30 previous Cops, taking in resolutions that were difficult to fit into the other formal negotiating strands.

Within the other strands at Cop31, there are still major disagreements among developed and developing countries. Poor nations are unhappy that no new finance is likely to be forthcoming at this Cop.

“Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Mvundla of groundWork, an environmental justice nonprofit in South Africa. “The global south is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”

The text contains items likely to be subject to trade-offs among parties. For instance, language calling for “carbon dioxide removal” was attacked by campaigners who see it as a “false solution”, but it is unlikely that some fossil fuel-producing countries would agree any text without such a reference.

Bowen also said fossil fuel-producing countries did not bear more responsibility than consumer countries in tackling the climate crisis. “There are two types of countries in the world, fossil fuel exporters and fossil fuel importers, and we’re all in it together. The idea that everything [is for] fossil fuel exporters is not one I support,” he said. “We’re all part of this process, and just dealing with one and not the other is not realistic.”

He refused to commit Australia, which is one of the world’s biggest producers of coal, to a phaseout of fossil fuel exports, as campaigners and some countries are calling for, but said Australia had a plan to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions and was adjusting for a world in which all countries did the same.

“I accept the logic that all countries will need to reduce emissions, and that means they’re reducing their use of fossil fuels, and that will impact on Australia’s exports, absolutely,” he said. “That’s why we’re preparing our economy for that change.”

articles.title: "Minacce russe non credibili, Ue non si faccia impressionare". Intervista a Gentiloni (VIDEO)
articles.summary: AGI - L’ Unione europea non dovrebbe farsi impressionare dalle "richieste impossibili o minacce improbabili" della Russia che paventa di “usare la forza contro l' Europa quando da cinque anni è impantanata in una guerra con l' Ucraina ”, una minaccia che “onestamente non è molto convincente". L'ex premier italiano e Commissario Ue Paolo Gentiloni , parlando con l'AGI a margine della seconda edizione del Lugano Global Forum , in corso nella città del Canton Ticino, spiega che i toni aggressivi e 'ultimativi' di Mosca nei confronti dell' Europa non lo colgono di sorpresa. "Non mi stupisce che la Russia abbia fatto filtrare la domanda di un arretramento della Nato nei confini che aveva alla fine del secolo scorso. Cose ridicole, ma che - osserva l'ex commissario Ue - fanno parte di una certa tradizione con la quale la Russia e, un tempo, l' Unione Sovietica , affrontano le dinamiche negoziali". La sostanza, osserva ancora Gentiloni , è infatti un'altra: "Mi sembra che comincia a farsi strada la possibilità di un negoziato e questo forse spiega anche questi toni ogni tanto estremi e minacciosi da parte russa ", conclude. Possibilità di negoziato e vertice trilaterale Parlando del primo vertice trilaterale dei leader di Usa , Cina e Russia , da giovedì a Shenzhen , Gentiloni ne sminuisce la portata, reale e potenziale: "Non mi aspetto grandi cose da questo incontro, che Putin ha fortemente voluto in Cina , perché al di là della 'photo opportunity' non credo che ci sarà sostanza". In vista dello storico trilaterale, Paolo Gentiloni afferma che "chi addirittura parla di una 'nuova Yalta' forse non ha capito in che mondo ci troviamo". In quanto alla possibilità che il vertice possa addirittura ridiscutere gli assetti della sicurezza europea , il giudizio è ancora più netto: ”È uno scenario ridicolo". Europa ai negoziati di pace Analizzando poi lo scenario che vedrebbe l' Ue, nel formato E-5 , al tavolo dei negoziati di pace tra Mosca e Kiev , Gentiloni spiega che "è ovvio che, se si andasse verso un negoziato, l' Europa ne farà parte". articles.title: Nvidia scandal: China's chips dilemma, US rivalry shape AI race
articles.summary: The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.
articles.preview: November 16, 2026 The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China. China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.
articles.body:
November 16, 2026

The controversy surrounding Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has put a spotlight on the intensifying AI race between the US and China.

China has ambitious plans to become the leader in the global race for artificial intelligence (AI). Beijing is aware that the country needs cutting-edge chips to achieve this goal.

Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, who chairs the Communist Party's Commission on Science and Technology, has been tasked with strengthening China's capacity for technological innovation, which would enhance its strategic competitiveness against the United States.

The party is currently using AI to monitor citizens, develop advanced unmanned weapons systems, and transform economic sectors through robotics and industrial automation, among other things.

But the US has so far been leading the way in manufacturing technology and chip design. And Washington has taken a slew of measures to retain its dominance in this strategic sector.

US moves to restrict China's access to chips

As early as 2023, the then Biden administration decided to restrict the export of advanced semiconductors and chip manufacturing equipment to China, citing national security reasons.

Beijing slammed the US restrictions, calling them "unilateral and arbitrary."

US chipmakers, however, have been drawn to China's vast and rapidly growing market.

Jensen Huang, who resigned as CEO of the American AI chip manufacturer Nvidia last week, enjoyed something of a rock star status in China. The 63-year-old, who was born in Taiwan, is viewed in China as a successful entrepreneur.

Huang, who has emerged as a key adviser on AI to US President Donald Trumpduring his second term, has pushed for looser regulations and fewer restrictions on selling AI chips to China.

In December, the Trump administration granted Nvidia permission to ship its H200 chips to China, provided the US got a 25% cut of sales.

Although the H200 is not part of Nvidia's highest-performance series, it is significantly more efficient than competing Chinese products.

Each of these chips carries a hefty $27,000 (€24,000) price tag, and Nvidia estimates demand in China at 2 million units, which corresponds to sales of approximately $5.4 billion from this product alone.

Nvidia affair and espionage allegations

But Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by the US of spying for Beijing.

The scandal not only sent shockwaves through the global AI and semiconductor industries, but also fueled highly contentious political debates in China and the US.

Washington, which sees its national security threatened, is said to be planning further restrictions against China to close loopholes that allow Chinese firms to acquire advanced American semiconductors.

China, on the other hand, denied it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang, saying the spying allegations were unsubstantiated and a smear campaign against Beijing.

Beijing also stepped up its rhetoric ahead of the meeting between President Xi Jinping and Trump at this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"China has consistently opposed the misuse of export control measures that jeopardize the stability of global industrial and supply chains, as this is not in the interest of either party," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on November 13.

Some Chinese media outlets have also criticized the reporting on the issue.

"Jensen Huang cheated on his wife. What does that have to do with China?" asked China's state-run Global Times newspaper in an editorial.

It accused the US media of turning the affair into a "Hollywood thriller" but without providing the "hard evidence to back up the central allegations."

Many Chinese have also taken to the microblogging and social media platform Weibo to comment on the controversy.

A user wrote that Huang's downfall was, in essence, "the result of political maneuvering within the United States," while another user asked: "Could a love affair really cause Mr. Huang to resign? Isn't this plot a little too melodramatic?"

Behind the verbal sparring lies an economic calculation.

Is China buying more US chips?

Ding, the Chinese vice premier, has to decide whether China should continue to rely on US chips or back its domestic industry in the hope that it can achieve the breakthrough needed to surpass American competitors.

Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 chips, for instance, are currently sitting in Hong Kong, awaiting Chinese import approval.

The White House has already given the green light, but Beijing has yet to approve the imports.

For Karson Elmgren, research manager at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy in Washington, that is puzzling. "To me, this suggests that China does not view short-term advantages as decisive and is confident in its ability to replace US chips over the medium term."

Chinese AI products are also increasingly using "Made in China" chips.

"This effectively mitigates the risks of cyberattacks by foreign actors," wrote Tiantian Wang of the Harbin Institute of Technology in a recent study on China's semiconductor strategy.

This is the case not only to civilian sectors. "Against the backdrop of the current complex geopolitical situation, strengthening autonomy and control over national defense and critical infrastructure has become a core element of the national security strategy," Wang explained.

According to her, for example, the radar systems in China's fifth-generation Chengdu J-20 fighter jet and in the Dongfeng-41 intercontinental ballistic missile are equipped exclusively with Chinese chips.

China is increasingly focused on autonomous AI chip platforms developed domestically, Wang underscored.

"This has created a closed ecosystem that encompasses data, algorithms, computing power, and chips, thereby reducing systemic dependence on foreign chips such as Nvidia," she added.

China lacks advanced chip-making equipment

However, China still lacks production equipment for state-of-the-art chips.

Chip manufacturing requires lithography systems that expose raw silicon materials to ultraviolet light.

Bowing to pressure from Washington, the Dutch maker of lithography machines, ASML, has stopped exporting its most advanced machines to China.

The ban helps secure the US's technological lead in AI chips, said the Center for Technology & Statecraft, a Washington-based think tank. If China were to import additional ASML systems like it did in 2024 and 2025, "its annual production could be sufficient to wipe out much of the US lead and, under certain scenarios, even surpass it."

According to the international consulting firm Deloitte, China is planning further extensive investments. "The focus is on supporting companies through long-term capital provision and research-oriented incentives to build sustainable innovation in key technologies."

Policymakers aim to stabilize the entire supply chain, expand self-sufficiency, and actively manage risks, the study noted. "The focus is shifting from supporting individual companies to fostering synergies within the supply chain, establishing quality systems, and ensuring the secure management of critical resources in order to promote the development of a more resilient industrial organizational structure."

This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Congo struggles to tame ebola outbreak six months into response
articles.summary: More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016
articles.preview: More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016
articles.body:
Ebola virus

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.

More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to government data. It is the deadliest of Congo’s 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities’ ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.

By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country’s 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.

New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.

Questions over funding and management

Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.

One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.

Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.

Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.

“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organization Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.

Children face high death rates

Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.

Most children affected by the disease have not received specialized care, contributing to high death rates.

According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through Nov. 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.

Conflict and attacks hamper response

Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.

Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.

The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.

Fighting between government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world’s most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.

The virus’s rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

The International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) had been expected to elect its secretary-general during the summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. articles.body:
OIF

A diplomatic dispute between the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) and Rwanda has forced a major summit of French-speaking nations to postpone the election of a new leader until the end of 2027.

The International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF) had been expected to elect its secretary-general during the summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. However, tensions escalated after DR Congo threatened to withdraw from the organisation if Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo secured a third term.

Speaking after the decision, Mushikiwabo acknowledged facing intense pressure but said she had maintained her candidacy because of her ambition to continue serving the organisation and her commitment to its reforms.

She said member states had agreed to postpone the election in the absence of consensus.

Tensions between the two African neighbours remain high, with Kinshasa accusing Kigali of supporting the M23 armed group, which has seized large areas of eastern DR Congo. Rwanda denies the allegations.

DR Congo’s potential departure would be a significant setback for the OIF. The country is home to millions of French speakers and is the organisation’s second-largest Francophone nation after France.

Mushikiwabo has confirmed she intends to remain a candidate when the election takes place at the end of 2027.

articles.body:
Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe".

The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.

They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.

On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.

The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website.

Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".

Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.

The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media.

Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions.

One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.

Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."

Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions.

Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.

Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

articles.body:
Israel

Two Israeli opposition leaders denounced Monday an "attempted coup" following press reports that outgoing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office tried to frame members of an Arab-Israeli party ahead of last month's election.

"As more and more details come to light, it becomes clear: This wasn't an attempt to disrupt the elections. It was an attempted coup," wrote Yair Lapid on X, who headed the opposition in the previous legislature and co-chairs the Beyachad list.

Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday that on the eve of the October 27 election, Netanyahu's chief of staff Ido Norden had phoned in a complaint to the police about members of the Arab-Israeli Raam party.

Norden reportedly pointed the police to a purported intelligence source - a former employee of Netanyahu's office - who provided information that led to the arrest of three Raam members.

The three men were later released when the police determined that the information was unfounded. Netanyahu subsequently accused Arab parties of electoral fraud after they gained a record number of seats.

His Likud party issued a statement denying the latest allegations.

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz also reported that David Zini, head of the Shin Bet domestic security service, sought to wiretap leaders of the other Arab slate, the Joint List, but the attorney general turned down his request due to lack of evidence.

Following the report, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen also denounced an "attempted coup by Netanyahu".

"If the findings are confirmed, this is a criminal mechanism that operated from the heart of government to rig the election results. Everyone found responsible must be held accountable, including Netanyahu," he wrote on X.

Raam's number two, former police chief Yoav Segalovitz, called for an urgent investigation.

"These suspicions require an immediate, independent and thorough criminal investigation that reaches everyone involved, at every level and in every role," he wrote on X.

"Netanyahu cried out that his election was being stolen, while he himself tried to steal the country and is still trying to do so now," he added.

Netanyahu's main rival, former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, wrote on Sunday that the caretaker prime minister "cannot remain at the head of the government for a minute longer".

Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's opposition secured the 61 seats required to form a government following last month's election.

The two Arab parties, the Joint List and Raam, have indicated support for Eisenkot.

articles.summary: The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie, comprising 53 members and dozens more associates, had intended to choose a new secretary general during talks in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh.
articles.preview: A summit of French-speaking nations attended by France's Emmanuel Macron postponed the election of a new chief on Monday, November 16, after a bitter row between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, African neighbors. The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), a post-colonial entity resembling the Commonwealth, comprising 53 members and dozens more associates, had intended to choose a new secretary general during talks in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh.
articles.body:
A summit of French-speaking nations attended by France's Emmanuel Macron postponed the election of a new chief on Monday, November 16, after a bitter row between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, African neighbors.

The Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF), a post-colonial entity resembling the Commonwealth, comprising 53 members and dozens more associates, had intended to choose a new secretary general during talks in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh.

But amid a walkout threat by DR Congo, delegates decided to postpone the election for a year, announced Secretary General Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda. Kinshasa had threatened to quit the OIF if Mushikiwabo was chosen for a third term on Monday, and had put forward its own candidate. She will remain in the post, but her country will not field a candidate at the next election, sources close to the matter told Agence France-Presse (AFP).

DR Congo accuses neighboring Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group, which has seized swathes of its territory, an allegation Kigali denies. The departure of DR Congo, the second most Francophone country after France with 57.3 million speakers, according to the OIF, would have been a major blow to the organization. Last year, Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso withdrew after successive coups that saw Paris-friendly governments replaced by pro-Russian juntas.

'Very sad day'

France's Macron, who attended the summit alongside DR Congo President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwanda's Paul Kagame, had earlier called for unity. A source in his office welcomed the postponement of the vote on Monday, saying it would allow time for reforms of the appointment process. "This solution makes it possible to overcome divisions and preserve consensus within the Francophone family," the source said, hailing members' "sense of responsibility."

Rwanda had earlier denounced Paris's involvement in the election, saying Macron asked Kagame to withdraw his candidate, a request it said it rejected. Paris later said it had suggested the withdrawal of both the Rwandan candidate and DR Congo's proposed choice, Juliana Lumumba, the daughter of national hero Patrice Lumumba.

Mushikiwabo denounced what she called "numerous and intense" pressures put on her to withdraw, and said she had wanted to stay "as a matter of principle." But DR Congo's Foreign Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner welcomed a "wise compromise" that would help "preserve the unity of the Francophonie," in a post on X.

The row revived debate over the influence of France, the former colonial ruler of many member states and the Francophonie organization's biggest donor. Former Romanian prime minister Dacian Ciolos, one of the four candidates for election, deplored a "very sad day" for the organization. "If we want the Francophonie to remain relevant, our absolute priority must be to rebuild trust among ourselves," he said in a statement.

Macron was not in Phnom Penh for the decision on the vote, having flown to Siem Reap with Cambodia's King Norodom Sihamoni to inaugurate an 11th-century temple at Angkor restored with French funds and expertise. West Mebon temple, which was built during the Khmer Empire, stands on an island in the middle of a reservoir at the UNESCO World Heritage site in western Cambodia.

articles.title: Le email dal Misoginistan
articles.summary: Per spaventare un paese intero sono bastati un account rubato e un elenco pubblico di indirizzi di posta elettronica. Il rischio ora è rispondere con tecnologie di sorveglianza costose e inutili

L’11 novembre 2026, verso le dieci del mattino, circa 6.300 scuole statali italiane hanno ricevuto la stessa email. Scritta con un tono tipico dello spam, annunciava un ordigno “con innesco a distanza” nascosto in un sacchetto di plastica, una bomba nell’auto “del vostro primo ministro” e varie atrocità: “di voi rimarranno solo le ossa e una poltiglia sanguinolenta”. Il messaggio era firmato da Mikhail Andropov, improbabile “leader del Vilayat di Misoginistan”.

A posteriori, l’email è un piccolo capolavoro di trollaggio che mette insieme tantissimi temi delicati su cui ci scontriamo ogni giorno finendo per non saper più distinguere vero e falso. È una minaccia-meme in cui ciascuno può vedere il nemico che vuole.

La procura di Milano ha aperto un’indagine; la presidente del consiglio Giorgia Meloni ha parlato di una “strategia volta a generare allarme e preoccupazione” e ha convocato le opposizioni; la deputata del Partito democratico Debora Serracchiani ha detto che “di fronte a un momento di tensione, a un terrorismo per ora solo psicologico, vorremmo un piano del governo chiaro”.

Per generare tutte queste reazioni ci è voluto davvero poco: sono bastati un account di posta e un file pubblico. L’account è stato rubato all’inizio dell’anno a un’ex studentessa della Da-Yeh, un’università privata di Taiwan che gestisce la posta con il software Microsoft 365. Il file pubblico, invece, è quasi sicuramente il portale di open data del ministero dell’istruzione. Secondo la ricostruzione del Post a conferma di questa ipotesi c’è il fatto che le scuole paritarie, quelle della Valle d’Aosta e quelle del Trentino-Alto Adige, che non condividono quei dati con il ministero, non hanno ricevuto niente.

Lo stesso giorno una minaccia identica è arrivata a centinaia di scuole in Irlanda, Irlanda del Nord e Scozia.

In mattinata la Garda, la polizia irlandese, ha diffuso un comunicato dicendo che la minaccia non era credibile e che non consigliava “a nessun istituto di evacuare” l’edificio. Il dipartimento dell’istruzione ha mandato una circolare alle scuole in giornata. Alcune scuole di Dublino, Wicklow e Cork hanno mandato comunque a casa gli studenti. In Irlanda del Nord la Education authority, l’ente che gestisce le scuole, ha detto subito che il messaggio somigliava alla bufala del mese prima e che non c’erano prove di una minaccia credibile.

Le scuole sono state invitate a restare aperte, salvo indicazioni diverse della polizia. In Scozia la polizia ha valutato i messaggi “immediatamente” e ha detto che non c’era bisogno di evacuare gli edifici né di tenere i bambini a casa. Alcune scuole della Scozia continentale hanno sgomberato lo stesso le aule. Nelle Shetland, invece, gli studenti sono rimasti in classe, ma alcuni genitori si sono lamentati di aver saputo della minaccia dai siti di notizie e non dalla scuola.

Per loro era almeno la terza ondata: prima c’è stato il caso di Antrim a maggio. Poi più di 150 scuole irlandesi il 14 ottobre e trecento nordirlandesi il 19 ottobre. Dopo il primo caso di ottobre il dipartimento dell’istruzione irlandese aveva cominciato a rivedere i protocolli. Il deputato Pádraig O’Sullivan, che aveva presentato un’interrogazione, aveva detto: “I consigli scolastici non dovrebbero essere lasciati a capire da soli cosa fare”.

In Italia molte scuole sono state evacuate, non senza polemiche e disorganizzazioni varie. Alcuni dirigenti scolastici hanno ritenuto che l’email fosse una bufala tipica di internet, come quelle email che annunciano un’imprevista eredità da un principe nigeriano. Altri hanno invece preferito fare degli accertamenti, evacuare le scuole o fare entrambe le cose.

Tutte le scelte sono state criticate e le critiche hanno il loro senso: da un lato forse si poteva intuire facilmente la bufala. Dall’altro, però, può prevalere il principio di precauzione: se una minaccia si fosse concretizzata, i commenti a posteriori – sempre deleteri – sarebbero stati di ben altro tono.

Non solo. C’è un protocollo: è previsto che, in caso di allarme bomba, la direzione della scuola chiami il 112 e, coordinandosi con le forze di polizia, attivi le procedure di evacuazione e di messa in sicurezza, secondo il Piano di emergenza ed evacuazione (Pee) che ogni scuola deve avere obbligatoriamente. Come abbiamo visto dalle diverse reazioni, è un protocollo che lascia molta discrezionalità. E forse è giusto che sia così.

Società fragili

Questa storia ricorda le recenti minacce agli aerei firmate dai “combattenti dello Stato maschile”: artigianato digitale di bassa lega con credenziali rubate, un elenco scaricabile, un fornitore di posta che ha lasciato partire migliaia di minacce identiche da un account violato. E, soprattutto, un’accozzaglia di temi sensibili che da anni vengono usati abitualmente anche dalla comunicazione istituzionale e dall’informazione per parlare di rischi, nemici, allarmi e possibili guerre in arrivo. In generale, per spaventarci.

Entrambe le situazioni, comunque, ti lasciano il dubbio che qualcosa di vero ci possa essere e rivelano la fragilità delle nostre società.

Fin qui le intelligenze artificiali c’entrano molto poco: non sono servite e non c’è stato nessun hackeraggio della pubblica amministrazione né una cattiva gestione dei dati.

Però bisogna fare attenzione alle soluzioni che verranno proposte. Dopo situazioni come questa arriva puntuale chi vende sicurezza “intelligente”. Negli Stati Uniti è un mercato vero e proprio e sappiamo già che le cose non vanno bene. A novembre del 2024 la Commissione federale per il commercio (Ftc) ha accusato la Evolv Technologies, i cui scanner con ia erano installati in più di ottocento scuole, di aver promesso prestazioni senza prove adeguate.

Nel 2022 uno di quegli scanner non aveva rilevato il coltello con cui uno studente è stato poi accoltellato. A ottobre del 2025, alla Kenwood high school, nella contea di Baltimora, un sistema della Omnilert ha segnalato come arma il sacchetto di patatine di farina di mais che uno studente teneva in mano. Per questo lo studente è stato ammanettato e perquisito. E secondo l’azienda il sistema ha “funzionato come previsto”.

La tentazione politica è prevedibile: rispondere a una minaccia – probabilmente inesistente – con tecnologie costose, opache e di sorveglianza. Telecamere con riconoscimento automatico, scanner all’ingresso, sensori nei bagni. Bisogna vigilare attentamente perché questo non accada.

Le ia, però, possono servire per altri scopi, con ambizioni molto più modeste ma anche molto più utili. Prima di tutto, possono aiutarci nel riconoscimento di questi fenomeni. La stessa email arrivata a seimila indirizzi istituzionali nel giro di pochi minuti è già un’informazione: si tratta di un invio di massa.

Un centro unico, gestito dal ministero con la polizia postale e l’Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale, potrebbe raccogliere le segnalazioni delle scuole e confrontarle in tempo reale. I modelli linguistici sono adatti a riconoscere lo stesso messaggio quando cambia lingua, firma o formulazione, e a collegarlo a campagne già viste, avendo accesso ai dati storici.

La firma di Andropov, per esempio, era già comparsa in falsi allarmi in Irlanda, nel Regno Unito e in Bulgaria. Tutto questo si può combinare con altri dati che dovrebbero essere a disposizione delle forze di polizia e aiutare a capire la probabilità che una minaccia sia credibile. La decisione resta comunque in capo a persone che si prendono la loro responsabilità. Ma le macchine possono accorciare i tempi di decisione.

Poi ci possono aiutare con la comunicazione. Come mi ha detto la docente e divulgatrice Anna Rita Longo, “ogni vuoto informativo viene riempito da ansia e angoscia”. L’11 novembre quel vuoto informativo è stato riempito in maniera confusa dalle chat di classe, dai titoli spaventosi sulla guerra ibrida, dalle dichiarazioni sulle strategie del terrore senza prove: davvero non possiamo sapere, in questo momento, chi ci sia dietro alla email. Potrebbe anche essere qualcuno che ha voluto solo divertirsi.

Invece di soffiare sul fuoco della paura, in futuro si potrebbe preparare un messaggio verificato da mandare in pochi minuti a tutte le famiglie, tradotto in più lingue, controllato da qualcuno prima dell’invio.

Infine, anche i grandi gestori di posta possono usare le ia per segnalare anomalie come un invio di massa da un unico account allo stesso tipo di destinatari.

Ma alla fine ci vuole l’umanità. Per esempio, costruire comunità più coese, in cui si smetta di prepararsi costantemente all’individuazione di un nemico, di odiare l’altro e di cercare il colpevole da criminalizzare per nascondere i problemi. È facile criticare le scelte di un dirigente scolastico dopo che le cose sono successe. Ma non si può lasciar fuori dall’analisi il contesto sociale. Temo però che per questo non basterebbero nemmeno le ia. ◆

articles.body:
Inside Story

There is division within the European Union over diplomatic strategy for efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian cities as Kyiv’s forces continue to carry out long-range strikes.

But diplomatic pressure is ramping up, too, with the European Union wanting a say in United States-brokered talks aimed at ending Russia and Ukraine’s four-and-a-half-year war.

So, what role should Europe play?

articles.title: Somali-American Uber driver left in coma after alleged hate crime in Minnesota
articles.summary: Somali-American Uber driver left in coma after alleged hate crime in Minnesota Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 18:46 Mohamed Yusuf was reportedly run over multiple times with his own vehicle after a passenger said he disliked his Muslim name A screenshot of a GoFundMe fundraiser launched to support Mohamed Yusuf, the Somali-American Uber driver who was the victim of a suspected hate crime in Minnesota Off A Somali-American Uber driver is fighting for his life after being strangled and repeatedly run over with his own vehicle, allegedly by a passenger in Minnesota, in an attack his family believes was motivated by anti-Muslim hatred. Mohamed Yusuf was working in Hopkins, a suburb of Minneapolis, early on Saturday when a passenger allegedly asked him his name before telling him he did not like the name "Mohamed". According to Yusuf's relatives, the passenger then allegedly choked him from behind, seized control of his vehicle and ran him over multiple times. "He was run over multiple times with his own vehicle," Yusuf's son, Mustafa Osman, told The Somali Brief . Yusuf was reportedly found in a ditch nearly a mile away, suffering from broken legs and ribs, two collapsed lungs, a spinal injury and internal bleeding. He remains hospitalised in a coma, according to his family. Hopkins police confirmed that officers responding to a report of a suspicious vehicle at around 1.20am on Saturday discovered a seriously injured man and subsequently took a male suspect into custody. According to the Times of India , arrest records show that a man identified as Samit Apurva Patel was taken into custody by Hopkins Police on 14 November on a first-degree assault charge. However, authorities have not confirmed whether Patel's arrest is connected to Yusuf's assault or publicly identified the suspect in the case. Police have also not established a motive or confirmed whether the incident is being investigated as a hate crime. The attack has sparked outrage among Somali and Muslim Americans, with community members demanding that authorities investigate it as a possible hate crime. US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar condemned the attack, warning that the continued dehumanisation of Somali Americans has real-world consequences. "This horrific act of racial violence is unacceptable," Omar wrote on X, adding that no one should live in fear because of their identity, while calling for an end to the hatred dividing communities. My heart is with Mohamed and his family. I am praying for his full recovery. This horrific act of racial violence is unacceptable. No one should live in fear because of who they are. The relentless dehumanization of the Somali community has real consequences. We must unequivocally condemn this violence and reject the hatred that divides our communities. — Ilhan Omar (@IlhanMN) November 15, 2026 Prominent Muslim-American scholar Omar Suleiman also responded, warning that attacks targeting the Somali community were becoming increasingly frequent. Suleiman said Yusuf had simply gone to work to provide for his family and was now fighting for his life, praying for his recovery and calling for accountability for those who spread hatred and those who act upon it. Attacks on our Somali community are more and more frequent. Mohamed Yusuf went to work to provide for his family and is now fighting for his life after a horrific attack. May Allah grant him a full recovery and hold accountable those who spread and act upon such hatred. — Dr. Omar Suleiman (@omarsuleiman) November 15, 2026 The case triggered widespread anger online about the atmosphere that allowed such attacks to happen across the United States. One of Yusuf’s family members took to X and said, “The passenger said he hated people named Mohamed. I'm angry at our government for feeding that hatred with its anti-Muslim and anti-Somali rhetoric.” My in law is in a coma after being strangled, run over with his own car and left in a ditch by an Uber passenger. I don't understand how anyone can do something so horrific to another person. He's one of the kindest people I know and has made me feel welcome in this family. He was just doing his job. The passenger said he hated people named Mohamed. I'm angry at our government for feeding that hatred with its anti Muslim and anti Somali rhetoric. I'm praying he makes a full recovery and comes home to his family. He and his family deserve justice for what was done to him. — atikh 🇸🇴 (@tikhbana) November 15, 2026 A GoFundMe created for Yusuf and his family has already raised over $140,000. 'Our politicians created this hostile environment' The attack comes amid heightened concerns over anti-Somali rhetoric in the United States, particularly in Minnesota, which is home to one of the country's largest Somali-American communities. President Donald Trump has repeatedly targeted Somali immigrants in his political rhetoric, while Republican politicians in Minnesota have also made inflammatory remarks about the community. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer recently claimed on a conservative podcast that Minnesota had effectively inherited Somalia's civil war. "Our politicians created this hostile environment," one of Yusuf's relatives told The Somali Brief, describing the assault as a hate crime. Speaking at a news conference outside Hennepin County Medical Center on Monday, Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Council on American-Islamic Relations' Minnesota chapter, blamed the attack on what he described as a sustained campaign of hatred and dehumanisation against Somali Americans. "For more than a year and a half, Muslims across this country, and specifically Somali Americans here in Minnesota nationwide, have lived in [an] unwritten climate of fear, hatred, bigotry and dehumanisation," Hussein said. "This rhetoric has built an environment that we are living in today, an environment which is what we believe has created this heinous attack that took place on Saturday night here in Minnesota," he said. Hussein acknowledged that police were still gathering evidence and urged anyone with information about the incident to contact the Hopkins Police Department. “At this time, we know that Yusuf was on the phone with a family member the entire time the incident was taking place. I do not know what the officials are ready to share yet. We know that they are working hard and we recognise that this case requires additional information,” he added. "This is one of the most heinous attacks that we have ever seen, and it has shocked the conscience of all of us. We know it did not happen in [a] vacuum. We know it happened in an environment that has been created, festered and driven,” Hussein said. Minnesota state Senator Omar Fateh also condemned the attack, calling for an immediate and transparent investigation. "Mohamed Yusuf should be home safe with his family, not fighting for his life after an attack fueled by hatred towards his Somali identity," Fateh wrote on social media. The news conference brought together community leaders, elected officials, including Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, and rideshare drivers demanding that authorities investigate the assault as a possible hate crime. Uber said it was "shocked and horrified" by the incident, adding that it had banned the rider from its platform and would cooperate with law enforcement. A fundraising campaign established to support Yusuf and his family had raised more than $140,000 by Sunday, as supporters rallied around the injured driver. Yusuf's family described him as a devoted father and hardworking man who was simply trying to earn a living and return home safely. articles.title: Trump: 'Putin non va all'affondo, vuole la fine della guerra'
articles.summary: 'Potrebbe essere più duro', a Shenzen non escluso un bilaterale. Potrebbe vedere anche Kim
articles.preview: Vladimir Putin "potrebbe francamente essere più duro con l'Ucraina" ma credo che "abbia fatto un piccolo passo indietro. Ritengo che voglia vedere la fine" della guerra. E' un Donald Trump sicuro di sé quello che parla con i giornalisti prima di imbarcarsi per l'Asia, dove l'Ucraina sarà uno dei temi centrali. E dove l'attende il cruciale trilaterale con Xi Jinping e Vladimir Putin mentre il suo inviato Jared Kushner pur riconoscendo che "un accordo definitivo richiederà decisioni difficili", torna a parlare di "progressi" per porre fine al conflitto.
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin "potrebbe francamente essere più duro con l'Ucraina" ma credo che "abbia fatto un piccolo passo indietro. Ritengo che voglia vedere la fine" della guerra. E' un Donald Trump sicuro di sé quello che parla con i giornalisti prima di imbarcarsi per l'Asia, dove l'Ucraina sarà uno dei temi centrali. E dove l'attende il cruciale trilaterale con Xi Jinping e Vladimir Putin mentre il suo inviato Jared Kushner pur riconoscendo che "un accordo definitivo richiederà decisioni difficili", torna a parlare di "progressi" per porre fine al conflitto.

Prima a Manila all'Asean e poi a Shenzhen all'Apec, il presidente anatra zoppa cerca il suo riscatto dopo la scottante sconfitta alle elezioni di metà mandato. Una soluzione del dossier Ucraina, al quale lavora senza grandi successi da quando si è insediato alla Casa Bianca, gli consentirebbe di prendersi una rivincita agli occhi del mondo. Kiev sarà al centro del possibile bilaterale di Trump e Putin in Cina, e del trilaterale in programma fra il leader del Cremlino, il presidente cinese e il commander-in-chief. "Discuteranno di pace globale, con scambi approfonditi sulla promozione della stabilità strategica nelle relazioni tra le grandi potenze", ha fatto sapere Pechino parlando di incontro di "portata storica". Dal vertice non sono attesi grandi risultati, anche se è stato preannunciato dal Cremlino un comunicato finale. Trump probabilmente solleverà il nodo del controllo delle armi nucleari e della proliferazione, ma dalla Casa Bianca non si prevede alcuna svolta. Per Xi il trilaterale è l'occasione di rafforzarsi sul palcoscenico mondiale, anche se l'incontro comporta non pochi rischi vista l'imprevedibilità di Putin e Trump.

Il presidente cinese vuole inoltre evitare un paragone con la conferenza di Yalta del 1945, durante la quale Pechino era assente, ed è consapevole del pericolo di associare la Cina alle guerre in Ucraina e in Iran, da cui finora si è tenuto alla larga. Per Putin l'incontro è l'occasione di una nuova riabilitazione nel panorama mondiale che potrebbe poi portarlo al G20 di Miami il 14-15 dicembre. "Decideremo dopo l'Apec" se partecipare, ha detto consigliere presidenziale russo, Yuri Ushakov. Trump con ogni probabilità tornerà a fare pressione su Putin per una sua partecipazione al vertice che si terrà nel suo Doral, per il quale - è il suo auspicio - sogna quella pace con l'Ucraina che lo farebbe entrare nella storia. Il presidente non ha mai nascosto di voler vedere chiuso in tempi stretti un conflitto che, come ha lui stesso ammesso, si è però rivelato molto più complicato del previsto. Nelle ultime settimane, complice anche il duro colpo delle midterm, il commander-in-chief ha intensificato gli sforzi con gli inviati Steve Witkoff e Jared Kushner in viaggio fra Washington, Abu Dhabi e Mosca a caccia di quella svolta che è ancora sfuggente.

A margine dell'Apec, Trump avrà anche il suo terzo faccia a faccia dell'anno con con Xi. Secondo quanto riferito dalla Casa Bianca, i due si confronteranno sugli scambi e sull'attuazione della tregua commerciale raggiunta nei mesi scorsi. Non è atteso alcun accenno invece su Nvidia, anche se il presidente americano non ha escluso del tutto di poter quanto meno sfiorare l'argomento con Xi senza però rovinare i rapporti o gettare un'ombra sul vertice dell'Apec, già offuscato dallo storico trilaterale dei presidenti russo, cinese e americano. Un'altra minaccia sulla visibilità del summit è il possibile incontro fra Trump e il leader nord coreano Kim Jong Un. "Potrei vederlo" in Cina, "potrebbe venire, dipende da Xi. Sarà un'ottima cosa. Abbiamo l'opportunità di raggiungere risultati", ha spiegato il presidente. Il commander-in-chief ha incontrato Kim tre volte durante il suo primo mandato, divenendo il primo presidente in carica ad aver mai calpestato il territorio della Corea del Nord. La possibile foto di famiglia di Trump con Putin, Kim e Xi potrebbe comunque esporre il presidente a forti critiche in casa, attirandogli l'ira anche dei falchi repubblicani e indebolendolo così ancora di più in un'America che lo ha bocciato non solo per le sue politiche interne ma anche per quelle all'estero.

articles.title: Nuova mail bombing alle scuole italiane, nessuna evacuazione
articles.summary: I presidi avvisano la polizia e seguono le direttiva del Viminale. Una raffica di occupazioni
articles.preview: Una nuova mail bombing è arrivata nella tarda mattinata alle scuole di varie città italiane. "Ho appena ricevuto l'incarico di piazzare e attivare un ordigno esplosivo nel vostro edificio - si legge nel messaggio di posta elettronico firmato M.A., iniziali di Mikhail Andropov firma comparsa nelle mail simili arrivate nei giorni scorsi - L'esplosione avverrà tra 40 minuti". I presidi stavolta si sono attenuti alle nuove direttive del Viminale e nessun istituto è stato evacuato.
articles.body:
Una nuova mail bombing è arrivata nella tarda mattinata alle scuole di varie città italiane. "Ho appena ricevuto l'incarico di piazzare e attivare un ordigno esplosivo nel vostro edificio - si legge nel messaggio di posta elettronico firmato M.A., iniziali di Mikhail Andropov firma comparsa nelle mail simili arrivate nei giorni scorsi - L'esplosione avverrà tra 40 minuti". I presidi stavolta si sono attenuti alle nuove direttive del Viminale e nessun istituto è stato evacuato. Il mittente delle email sarebbe riconducibile ad un unico indirizzo che rimanda al Dipartimento per gli affari accademici e l'assicurazione della qualità dell'Università vietnamita di Da Nang, in Vietnam. Si tratta del terzo caso in pochi giorni e come nei casi precedenti è ipotizzabile che l'account sia stato hackerato.

Le indagini della Polizia Postale sono in corso e andrà capito se, come già nei precedenti casi, la mail provenga appunto da un indirizzo hackerato o se sia stata usata una VPN che nasconde l'indirizzo di provenienza. In base alle nuove linee guida, di fronte a mail seriali e prive di riscontri oggettivi, non scatta più l'evacuazione automatica degli edifici ma le segnalazioni vengono subito prese in carico dalle questure e dalla Polizia Postale. L'email in questione conteneva una novità rispetto alle due dei giorni scorsi, ovvero un riferimento anche alle mense scolastiche. Tuttavia il fatto non ha colto impreparati i dirigenti scolastici che si sono attenuti alle nuove disposizioni e non hanno perso la calma. Solo in pochi casi c'è stata una interruzione precauzionale del servizio mensa che poi, dopo i controlli, è ripreso regolarmente. Nella email si legge infatti anche: "Abbiamo reclutato un dipendente della vostra mensa, che ha mescolato al cibo e alle provviste una miscela tossica a base di azoturo di sodio e cianuro di potassio". "E' l'ennesima email con messaggi farneticanti e grotteschi - ha detto all'ANSA il presidente dei presidi di ANP, Antonello Giannelli - Sono contenuti che vanno ignorati e girati alla polizia postale e così hanno fatto i colleghi". Tra gli istituti romani ai quali è stata recapitata l'email e che ha sospeso, precauzionalmente, il servizio mensa, c'è l'istituto comprensivo Hypatia a Tor Bella Monaca, che conta 940 allievi. Ma, come ha spiegato la dirigente, Annalisa Laudando all'ANSA, una volta effettuati i controlli, tutti gli alunni hanno regolarmente pranzato. Sulla vicenda è intervenuto anche il ministro degli Esteri Antonio Tajani, il quale ha spiegato che in Europa si lavorerà sempre di più insieme contro gli attachi hacker. "In Italia è stato respinto quest'altro attacco di spam di mail, nessuna scuola è stata chiusa perché si trattava di una falsa minaccia. Però l'obiettivo era quello di continuare a provocare caos", ha detto. Prosegue intanto l'ondata di occupazioni di istituti in tutta Italia. Mentre alcuni studenti 'disoccupano', consentendo la ripresa delle lezioni, altri istituti superiori vengono occupati da nord a sud. Gli studenti lamentano mancanza di investimenti per la scuola, risorse buttate per le armi e angoscia per il futuro.

articles.title: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
articles.summary: US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran's influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group.
articles.preview: US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran’s influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group around the town of Jurf al-Nasr. Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).
articles.body:
US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran’s influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group around the town of Jurf al-Nasr.

Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area.

The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq.

Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar.

Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.

Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.

Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.

“We are therefore being subjected to the greatest campaign of blackmail aimed at forcing us to relinquish the weapons of dignity that have upheld sovereignty and protected the rights of Iraqis at multiple stages,” the group said in a statement.

The campaign to stamp out the oil smuggling trade has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of senior government officials and security directors.

Al-Aboudi said an investigative committee, following an intelligence agency report, had “detected clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, as well as attempts to bury and conceal traces of that tampering”.

Sources told the Reuters news agency that the smuggling, carried out with accomplices among some security and oil officials, has robbed the government of hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds, analysts believe the oil probe is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus.

Iranian-backed armed groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted repeated calls by both al-Zaidi and his ally, US President Donald Trump, to disarm.

They have struck US troops and targets in Saudi Arabia and the UAE in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

articles.title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
articles.summary: The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war.
