articles.body:
The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war.

Tehran, Iran – Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years.

Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries.

The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war.

Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes.

According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028.

Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap.

Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants resort to burning cheap fuel, predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air.

Despite that, Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi, a deputy energy minister, told the state-linked ILNA outlet on Saturday that mazut burning would continue this year.

Umud Shokri, energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said that if the problems facing Iran’s gas industry remain unresolved over the coming years, the consequences would extend beyond the energy sector, affecting industrial production, employment, inflation, and living standards.

“In my view, Iran’s biggest challenge is not a lack of energy resources, but its inability to turn those resources into reliable supplies for its people and economy,” Shokri told Al Jazeera. “Without serious reforms, sustained investment, and better energy management, what is now largely a seasonal crisis could gradually become a year-round problem.”

Shortages possible across Iran

Gas accounts for 73 percent of Iran’s energy mix, the gas company’s Tavakoli said last week, adding that household consumption had reached 480 million cubic metres per day and was expected to sharply rise as the cold season approaches.

Last winter’s peak consumption for households, businesses and small industries was recorded at 737 million.

The National Iranian Gas Company identifies 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces as considerably vulnerable to shortages this winter, particularly some provinces to the north of the country, including Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. High consumption due to cold temperatures, as well as locations near the ends of transmission lines, increase gas pressure problems in those provinces.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani explicitly warned during a press conference last week that if consumption grows, gas might be cut off across the country, including Tehran.

“Unlike electricity, which can be reconnected quickly after being cut off, bringing back gas after cutoff is a time-consuming process,” she said. “So, network stability is of utmost importance and we must work to prevent any disruptions.”

The government has said it will do its best not to let households or industries go offline due to gas shortages. But on Saturday, the Zagros Petrochemical Company, operating in southern Iran’s energy production hub of Asaluyeh, notified its shareholders that it shut down a methanol production unit until further notice in line with directives from the National Iranian Gas Company

David Jalilvand, managing director at Orient Matters, a geopolitical research consultancy in Germany, said the industrial sector would bear the brunt of the shortages as the authorities prioritise households, which rely on gas for heating.

“Prioritising households, however, does not guarantee that residential supplies will remain uninterrupted if shortages become severe,” he told Al Jazeera.

To help save on gas, the government has tasked its affiliated executive bodies with reducing their gas consumption by 20 percent. It has also said offices are obligated to keep their temperatures at around 18 degrees Celsius (64 degrees Fahrenheit), while homes are advised to maintain 18-21C (64-70F). Offices must also switch heating off on holidays.

The government said inspections last week led to disconnections at the Education Ministry building and five other government buildings in Tehran that were not complying with the energy-saving directives.

The government has also been struggling with a lingering petrol supply imbalance, and imposed sporadic power blackouts to cover electricity production shortfalls during summer and early autumn. In addition to raising the price of petrol twice in less than a year, the government has also significantly limited monthly petrol quotas allocated to personal vehicles.

Authorities have repeatedly asked Iranians to help offset the shortages by consuming less, while saying more price hikes are possible over the coming months.

An October directive also required eligible civil servants to work from home at least two days a week and encourage commuting without private cars on one day a week, as part of efforts to reduce fuel consumption.

“We must speak to the people honestly and explain we are facing gas shortages due to previous years’ imbalances and also damages from the war, so we need to save on gas,” First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said last week.

High-consuming users have also been told their gas prices will increase exponentially if they do not reduce consumption.

Jalilvand, from Orient Matters, said developing the South Pars gasfield, the world’s largest offshore natural gasfield shared between Iran and Qatar, has been cruicial in addressing the key challenge of keeping the supply of gas growing in line with domestic demand.

But he said sustaining production growth increasingly depends on addressing technical challenges that require foreign investment and technology.

“An equally important challenge lies on the demand side. Iran has enormous potential to improve energy efficiency, but realising it requires investment, technology and domestic policy reforms, particularly to address heavily subsidised energy prices.

“Reintegration into the global economy would make it considerably easier to finance and implement these improvements.”

Hamed, who runs a small apartment hotel in the northern province of Mazandaran, said his business experienced a drop in gas pressure last year, depsite not being a heavy consumer. But there were no total cutoffs.

He told Al Jazeera that lower-pressure gas can impact his business by affecting heating in guest rooms, disrupting the boiler for hot water used for showers and sanitation, and most of the hotel’s kitchen operations.

“It’s basically everything; I really hope it doesn’t come to that this year,” he said.

articles.title: Iran's growing exodus of young talent
articles.summary: Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.
articles.preview: November 16, 2026 Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country. "I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW. Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.
articles.body:
November 16, 2026

Conflict and uncertainty are driving more and more educated young Iranians to consider leaving the country.

"I had actually decided to leave Iran back in 2023," a physician in her mid-30s, who wished to remain anonymous, told DW.

Her decision followed the 2022 death in police custody of 22-year-old Iranian-Kurdish woman Jina Mahsa Amini, who had been arrested by Iran's so-called morality police for allegedly violating the country's strict dress code.

Amini's death sparked widespread protests and inspired the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which challenged authorities' enforcement of Iran's hijab mandate.

The physician said that the US-Israel war with Iran ultimately accelerated her plans to leave her homeland. She has been living with her family in a rented apartment in Turkey since early summer. From there, they hope to continue on to Germany.

"It took two years for my professional qualifications to be recognized in Germany. After that, I applied for an appointment at the German Embassy in Tehran," the physician said.

"Then the 12-day war broke out in the summer of 2025. The embassy closed and suddenly we were all left in limbo, not knowing what would happen next."

She became concerned after the US and Israel launched fresh airstrikes on Iran on February 28, 2026 — not just about the escalating conflict, but also about the prospect of internal unrest and political instability.

Turkey as a stopover

"Like many others we encountered during the emigration process, we decided to first move to a neighboring country," she said. "The plan was to stay in a third country for six months and then apply for a visa through the German embassy there. That's why my family and I came to Turkey."

Turkey is one of the few countries that allows Iranian citizens to enter without a visa for up to 90 days.

Since the latest conflict began, thousands of Iranians have crossed the border into Turkey. Many are trying to secure their stay through residence permits rather than seeking asylum.

According to official Turkish statistics, nearly 100,000 Iranian citizens were residing there in 2025. Among them are many academics and skilled professionals hoping to settle permanently in Europe or North America, seeing little future for themselves in Iran's war-hit economy.

A US naval blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf over the past few months has disrupted oil exports, trade and government revenues. The turmoil has compounded the impact of decades of sanctions and economic mismanagement.

The situation has put most businesses under pressure by restricting access to foreign currency and raw materials, among other problems, threatening revenues and jobs.

The worsening conditions have left many people struggling to afford food, housing, health care and education.

The physician said the situation at the German embassy in Tehran, however, has improved in recent months. Some of her unmarried friends, who also initially moved to Turkey and spent substantial sums maintaining their stay there, have already returned to Iran to submit new visa applications from home.

She and her husband, however, have decided to stick to their original plan and wait out the six-month residency period in Turkey despite the difficulties.

"I can't and don't want to go to Germany without my family. I don't know how long it would take for them to receive family reunification visas," she explained. "And I don't know what might happen in the meantime. A new war could break out at any moment."

Young Iranians lose faith in the future

The departure of highly qualified professionals and students has become one of the most pressing challenges facing Iranian society. Today, there are few families in which someone has not already emigrated or is not at least considering doing so.

A 2025 study by the University of Guilan in Iran examined the relationship between opportunities for social participation and students' willingness to emigrate.

The researchers found a statistically significant correlation: Students who felt they had fewer opportunities to shape their future in Iran were more likely to consider emigrating.

Economic concerns are only part of the picture. Limited political participation, social restrictions and a sense of powerlessness are also driving many young Iranians to leave.

Mahsa, who is in her mid-20s, told DW that she has already secured admission to a German university.

Ali, meanwhile, dreams of a life outside Iran. The 23-year-old holds a bachelor's degree in engineering and is currently preparing for the entrance exam for a master's program at a public university. His long-term goal is to obtain a stronger qualification and then leave Iran — ideally with a scholarship.

"That's my dream of a better future," he said.

This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan
articles.summary: The paper trail that leads from the UAE to a dead boy in Sudan Submitted by Ahmed Ismat Ahmed on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 14:01 The RSF killed Osama, my little brother's 12-year-old best friend. This is what made it possible Osama (r) and his best friend Mohammed, pictured a week before the war in Sudan began in April 2023 (Ahmed Ismat Ahmed/MEE) On Osama was my younger brother’s best friend. He was 12. The Rapid Support Forces killed him when they attacked a town in al-Jazira state , Sudan , in 2023. The two of them used to share the same bicycle - one pedalling, the other running beside it, hand on the seat. Then one of them simply stopped existing. After the Khartoum sit-in was broken in the spring of 2019 and the resistance committees - nationwide groups of local activists of which I was a part - moved into the neighbourhoods, a few of us found ourselves guarding wool. Eid was coming. Families who could still afford it had bought sheep. When the slaughtering was done, the wool was left in the open lot where we used to meet. Someone said it was a waste to sell it in small piles for almost nothing. Someone else said the locality had not touched the streetlights on our main road in months. Children fell when it rained. Old people stopped walking to the mosque after dark because they could not see the path. We gathered the wool and took turns sitting with it at night. When the money came - folded, counted twice - we sat down and wrote it into a cheap notebook with a blue cover. I learned early that there are two kinds of paperwork. They do not answer to the same people Different hands. The wool money. The cost of the generator. Who had counted. The names of the boys who brought something. The phone numbers of mothers to call if something went wrong. Nobody set out to make an archive. It became one because no other archive had space for us. We used the money to fix the streetlights. History will not cite that notebook. But it is the only place where the fact that our street was lit again was written down correctly, by people who had to explain every pound to each other the next morning over tea. A ledger for Osama I learned early that there are two kinds of paperwork. They do not answer to the same people. One kind has to answer. The other is the paperwork of governments that still need other governments to believe them. Press releases. Treaties. Licences that other capitals accept as ordinary, even when the documents make plundering look like regular business. Purely humanitarian, they will tell you. It is one of the oldest lines in that second ledger. Read the record in the order it happened, not the order it was announced. On 5 December 2022, the Sudanese military and the civilian political bloc signed a Framework Agreement . This agreement said that the RSF, a paramilitary created in 2013 out of the Janjaweed militias that had killed hundreds of thousands in Darfur, would be folded into the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF). The Amdjarass airbase in Chad with an Ilyushin Il-76D aircraft on the tarmac, on 30 August 2023 (CreditHandout/2025 Planet Labs PBC/AFP) Three weeks later, on 28 December , Chad inaugurated a 3km-long paved runway in Amdjarass, a town 50km from the Sudanese border. The Chadian ministry’s own papers show the runway had been under construction since 2016 and was already 93 percent finished before anyone had agreed to call what was coming to Sudan a war . No public record names the United Arab Emirates as the runway’s builder. What the Emirates needed was only that the strip already be there - long enough and strong enough for the heavy cargo aircraft that leave from Al Dhafra, the Abu Dhabi airbase. Gold leaving Africa for the UAE (Swissaid) Through the whole of 2022, the UAE had already taken close to 40 tonnes of Sudanese gold . More than $2bn. None of it passed through a budget any Sudanese civilian had ever voted on. In March 2023, weeks before the fighting started , Sudan’s own central bank put $50m into Alkhaleej Bank. The United States Treasury later confirmed the bank was controlled by the RSF. Companies tied to the family of Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo , the RSF chief better known as Hemedti, hold more than 60 percent of the shares. The bank did not need a stolen signature. It needed one man willing to work both sides of the ledger before the rest of the world agreed to call it a war. Supplying a war By the time the first shot was fired in Khartoum on 15 April 2023, the RSF already had an airstrip the army did not share, a bank account the army’s own central bank had just finished refilling, a company that had been buying its vehicles for four years, and a gold trade larger than most of the ministries in the Sudanese capital put together. A flag is not power. A ministry is not power. Power is the money, the weapons, and the roads that carry both. By December 2022, that power had already changed hands. When Amdjarass began to draw attention , the airbridge did not stop. It moved. Kufra in southern Libya became the new node. Ethiopia the eastern blade . The thing was never a single pipeline that could be cut. It was a system that could be copied. The Ethiopian army base at Asosa providing support for Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, shown on 29 March 2026 (Imagery © 2026 Planet Labs/Analysis Yale HRL/MEE) I know something about denial. In September 2024, months after a UN panel of experts had set out a credible case that the UAE was arming the RSF, Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh wrote to a magazine under her own name and said it was not true. The Emirates, she wrote, had supplied no weapons at all . Nusseibeh had been her country’s ambassador to the United Nations from 2013 to 2024. Eleven years in that room teach a particular skill: not when to look away, but how much looking away a career can absorb before someone notices the pattern. news

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune on Sunday threatened to take action against drugs at "the source" amid longstanding accusations by Algiers that neighbouring Morocco was behind drug trafficking into the country.

Tebboune did not name Morocco in an address at the Algerian Supreme Court, but Algiers has often blamed Morocco as being the source of drugs trafficked through their shared border. "It's a war declared against Algeria, and when there's war the army is of course at the front line," Tebboune said. "If necessary, we can go further, even to the source of the drugs' production, in legitimate self-defence."

On Thursday, authorities said they destroyed nearly 10 tonnes of recently seized cannabis resin as well as 33 million psychotropic pills, although it remained unclear where the drugs had come from. Relations between Algeria and Morocco have been tense since Algiers severed diplomatic ties in 2021.

Last month, Tebboune also said drug trafficking into Algeria was part of a "hybrid war" waged by "saboteurs", although he again did not name any actors. The Algerian defence ministry regularly announces confiscating large amounts of drugs, with statements often saying they came from Morocco.

articles.title: ICC judges order end to investigation into alleged crimes by US forces in Afghanistan
articles.summary: ICC judges order end to investigation into alleged crimes by US forces in Afghanistan Submitted by Sondos Asem on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 10:56 The decision, signalled in an order first reported by MEE in August, raises questions over whether the court is seeking to ease US pressure following sanctions Rosario Salvatore Aitala, now presiding judge of the ICC’s Pre-Trial Chamber II, at his swearing-in ceremony in The Hague on 9 March 2018 (ICC/Flikr) Off Judges at the International Criminal Court (ICC) have ordered the closure of the court’s Afghanistan investigation that covered alleged war crimes by US forces, despite ongoing attempts by prosecutors to appeal the decision. Ending the investigation into alleged US crimes addresses one of Washington ’s longstanding objections to the ICC and one of the reasons behind the sanctions on the court and its officials. The move is therefore likely to raise questions about whether the court is seeking to ease tensions with Washington by signalling that it will no longer pursue allegations against US forces and their allies. The Afghanistan situation at the ICC dates back to November 2017, when then-prosecutor Fatou Bensouda first requested authorisation to investigate alleged crimes committed since 2003, including by Afghan and US forces as well as the Taliban and the IS-K group. That request was initially rejected by a differently composed pre-trial chamber in 2019, before the appeals chamber overturned the decision in March 2020 and authorised the investigation to proceed. Bensouda was sanctioned by the US government a few months later over alleged attempts to subject Americans to the court's jurisdiction. Members of the appeals chamber that authorised the decision were also later sanctioned. Afghanistan II launched In November 2024, six states - Chile, Costa Rica, Spain, France, Luxembourg and Mexico - jointly referred allegations of crimes against women and girls committed since the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, asking prosecutors to fold them into the existing Afghanistan investigation. The latest decision , dated 12 November, closes the strand of the Afghanistan probe that covered the conduct of US forces and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province group, known as IS-K. However, it leaves open the part of the inquiry that prosecutes the Taliban for crimes against humanity allegedly committed against women and other groups while acting as the de facto government of Afghanistan. ICC confirms Middle East Eye reporting on Afghanistan arrest warrants hanistan II, launched by judges on 20 October. Judges have also ordered relevant records, including four Taliban arrest warrants , transferred to that investigation. The move echoes previous ad ordered prosecutors to separate the Taliban investigation from the broader Afghanistan inquiry. The judges argued that the post-2021 conduct by the Taliban is "materially different" from the armed conflict-related violence that defined the original investigation authorised in 2020. MEE also reported at the time that judges pointed prosecutors towards a newly introduced procedure for closing the original investigation, the one that nominally covers alleged crimes by all parties, because it sat dormant for years. Sources familiar with the Afghanistan inquiry previously told MEE that the Office of the Prosecutor (OTP) had appealed two of the chamber’s previous decisions: the order to open a separate Taliban investigation and the order transferring court records to it. Those appeals are still pending before the appeals chamber. The OTP has also appealed the latest closure decision. Dialogue with the US MEE reported in December that diplomats at the ICC's annual Assembly of States Parties (ASP) meeting in The Hague said the Trump administration had pressed the court to drop its investigations into Afghanistan and Palestine as a condition for lifting sanctions. It also demanded that states amend the ICC’s founding treaty - the Rome Statute - to prevent the prosecution of nationals from countries that aren’t members of the court, such as the US and Israel . Netherlands denies active talks with US over curbing ICC powers to lift sanctions to rule out the suggestion that discussions were taking place with Washington over sweeping restrictions on the ICC. A Dutch foreign ministry spokesperson subsequently told MEE there were “no direct negotiations with the US” on amending the Rome Statute or closing any investigations. The spokesperson said the government was exploring the scope for dialogue with non-member states, but that a US-states parties dialogue had yet to take shape. The idea of dialogue with the US was floated in last year’s ASP in December after an EU diplomat presented the US demands for discussion. MEE revealed at the time that member states disagreed on what such a dialogue would entail, and by the end of the conference agreed that any dialogue should aim at ensuring the independence and effectiveness of the court. The court’s member states are due to meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December. Grace period for new sanctions Washington on 9 October imposed institutional sanctions on the ICC, while granting the court a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands. Once fully in effect, the measures could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations. The pre-trial chamber's decision in July to split the Afghanistan investigation came days after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to “dismantle the ICC, brick by brick”, in remarks referencing the court's 2020 decision authorising an investigation into alleged crimes committed in Afghanistan. Since February 2025, the US has imposed retaliatory financial and visa sanctions on court officials in connection with the Afghanistan and Palestine investigations, citing efforts to prosecute nationals or allies of the US, in particular Israel. ​​The first target was Karim Khan , the former prosecutor of the ICC, who was controversially removed by member states in July after an 18-month-long misconduct probe. Also targeted were nine judges, three of whom - Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Luz Ibanez - were members of the 2020 Appeals Chamber that authorised the Afghanistan investigation. The sanctions came despite the decision by Khan in 2021 to deprioritise the probe concerning US military and CIA personnel, as well as former Afghan government forces, in order to focus the investigation on the Taliban and the Islamic State-Khorasan Province. articles.body:
Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.

The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.

Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people.

The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war.

The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.

The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.

Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate has responded to a BBC request for comment.

Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.

Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.

Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.

Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect.

Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member.

The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia.

The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.

A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US.

But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input.

"We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov.

EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

articles.title: Come è nata la falsa notizia del blackout globale del 17 novembre
articles.summary: È un allarme privo di prove che fa leva sulla preoccupazione dei recenti attacchi informatici
articles.preview: Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.
articles.body:
Sono giorni che, sui social media, circolano post in cui si avverte di un possibile blackout mondiale che si dovrebbe verificare martedì 17 novembre. Questi contenuti allarmistici non spiegano mai bene le cause del blackout, ma descrivono uno scenario in cui le città saranno paralizzate e la popolazione resterà al buio, senza elettricità, senza Internet, con conti bancari bloccati e trasporti pubblici inaccessibili per 72 ore. Le persone vengono quindi fortemente invitate a fare scorte di contanti, acqua ed alimenti non deperibili.

Un allarme che fa leva sulla preoccupazione degli attacchi informatici delle scorse settimane in diversi Paesi europei, dei (falsi) allarmi bomba negli aeroporti e nelle scuole, e del problema informatico che ha bloccato per diversi tempo i servizi di Microsoft.

Ma di questo blackout del 17 novembre, non esistono prove. Questa storia, del tutto infondata, è nata travisando alcuni eventi recenti reali. Il primo riguarda le nuove linee guida della Commissione europea, presentate lo scorso 3 novembre al Forum europeo sulla protezione civile, per aiutare le persone a prepararsi alle emergenze ed essere autosufficienti per 72 ore, durante i primi giorni di un’eventuale crisi. Le linee guida arrivano a seguito dell’approvazione a marzo 2025 della Strategia dell’Unione europea in materia di preparazione. La Commissione ha proposto anche l’istituzione di una Giornata europea della preparazione alle emergenze, ma a partire dal prossimo anno, il 2027, e il 23 ottobre (non il 17 novembre). Da tempo documenti delle istituzioni europee o frasi dei suoi rappresentanti vengono manipolati in rete per diffondere tesi complottistiche di vario genere.

La data del 17 novembre ipotizzata dai contenuti social allarmistici arriva invece dagli Stati Uniti. Nel Paese, infatti, martedì le emittenti radiofoniche e televisive interromperanno la normale programmazione per trasmettere un messaggio di prova. Si tratta di un test triennale per verificare la funzionalità del sistema di allarme in caso di una reale emergenza nazionale. A svolgerlo sarà l’Ente federale per la gestione delle emergenze (FEMA), e ne aveva dato annuncio lo scorso settembre la Commissione federale per le comunicazioni (FCC).

Secondo poi diversi post questo fantomatico blackout globale del 17 novembre sarebbe stato profetizzato dai Simpson. Un episodio della serie televisiva statunitense – a cui sono stati attribuiti poteri divinatori per alcune coincidenze con la realtà – avrebbe infatti rivelato questa data di un prossimo blackout. Si tratta del settimo episodio della 35ª stagione, andato in onda originariamente il 19 novembre 2023 e intitolato “It’s a Blunderful Life”, in cui una Lisa Simpson adulta ripensa a un’interruzione di corrente che lasciò Springfield al buio per sei giorni, avvenuta proprio il 17 novembre.

Tuttavia, nell’episodio non viene specificato l’anno del blackout, e l’interruzione di corrente – della durata di sei giorni – termina il Giorno del Ringraziamento. Nel 2026 però questa festività cade il 26 novembre, ovvero 9 giorni più tardi la data del blackout ipotizzato. Inoltre, nell’episodio il blackout colpisce solo la cittadina di Springfield e non tutto il pianeta. Anche questo caso rientra quindi nel filone disinformativo che attribuisce ai Simpson poteri divinatori a causa di alcune coincidenze occorse nelle oltre 700 puntate andate in onda.

articles.title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians
articles.summary: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal. Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza. Continue reading...
articles.preview: Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal. Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza. Continue reading...
articles.body:
The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.

The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.

The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the company’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.

The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.

The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.

It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.

However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

In the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”

An embrace of big tech

In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.

The soldiers were exploring ways to use the company’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources said.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

The foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened new datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

‘The plan was to migrate everything’

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.

The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said: “The plan [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”

A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.

The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

In Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources said.

The checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders said the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

- Harry Davies is one of the Guardian producers on NAZA, which Yuval Abraham co-directed. NAZA is now in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the Guardian’s website from early December. Sign up here to be the first to watch it

articles.body:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

articles.title: Scattered by war, the band that gave voice to Sudan's revolution plays again
articles.summary: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.preview: The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered his 'Aswat al-Madina' (Arabic for Voices of the City) band across continents
articles.body:
Sudan

The Cairo studio where Sudanese musician Mohamed al-Mustafa strums his guitar is a long way away from the Khartoum protests where his band once performed for thousands demanding democracy, before war scattered them across multiple continents.

After living through revolution, war and years of displacement, Mustafa and his fellow musicians in "Aswat al-Madina" (Arabic for Voices of the City) have reunited in the Egyptian capital, returning to both recording and live performance.

"I still can't quite process the fact that we're back together," said Mustafa, the band's guitarist and co-founder, who goes by Timon.

"It still feels unreal," he told AFP between recording takes, as back home war rages between the two forces Sudan's youth once rallied against: the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

In the studio, old stories and songs transport the musicians back to Khartoum, where they became the soundtrack to Sudan's 2018 uprising against longtime ruler Omar al-Bashir.

Two days before war erupted between the army and the RSF, former allies who worked together to derail Sudan's transition to democracy, the band was debating setlists for their next performance.

Instead, they found themselves swept up in the conflict, which has since devastated Sudan, killing tens of thousands of people and displacing millions more.

'Never left me'

Founded in Khartoum in 2014, Aswat al-Madina was part of a wave of underground bands pushing Sudanese music beyond conventional boundaries.

Blending folk traditions with jazz, reggae and contemporary rhythms, they sang about corruption, social injustice and life under authoritarian rule.

"Before the revolution, we used a technique where everyone understood what we meant, but nobody could prove it," said lead singer Ibrahim Ahmed Taha, who was arrested several times over their music.

When Sudan's youth took to the streets in December 2018, demanding an end to Bashir's rule, the band's songs blasted from phones, passing cars and makeshift barricades.

Timon still remembers one demonstrator carrying a giant speaker blaring their music through the marches.

"The music pushed people forward. It told them not to retreat in the face of repression.

"That image has never left me."

The band was a regular fixture at pro-democracy protests, including at the sit-in outside military headquarters in Khartoum, where protesters gathered each evening to listen to speeches, poetry and music.

"Find me in the square at half-past revolution; tonight, the devil falls," one track goes.

That sit-in became the site of a massacre in June 2019, when security forces led by the military and the RSF killed at least 120 protesters.

Four years later, when those same forces turned their guns on each other, the band -- like many Sudanese - lost everything.

From their five-storey creative hub, "everything was gone," Timon said.

"Not just the musical equipment. Even the chairs and tables had been looted."

"You'd step into the street and see bodies lying there and buildings reduced to rubble. That's when you realise everything has fallen apart," Timon said.

As fighting spread, the musicians fled Sudan, carrying little more than backpacks and laptops.

'In Khartoum again'

Timon escaped to the United Arab Emirates while others settled in Egypt and elsewhere in Africa. Regular rehearsals gave way to anxious discussions of visas and relatives still trapped in Sudan.

It was only this August that the band could reunite in Cairo, for its first performance since the war began.

As familiar songs filled the venue, audience members sang along to every word, shouting requests.

"For a moment," Taha said, "I felt like I was in Khartoum again."

For keyboard player Roba Bashir, the band's only woman member, the reunion was "the happiest day since the war began".

Musab Mahgoub, who has attended two of the band's Cairo concerts since August, said the performances "brought back so many old memories of Sudan".

The band now hopes to tour internationally and is recording a new version of their song "Nos Kobayet Shai Bi'Aisha" ("Half a Cup of Tea with Bread") with an Egyptian-Nubian collaborator, its themes of home and family taking on special meaning in exile.

articles.title: Sudan and Ethiopia trade accusations over armed groups
articles.summary: Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighboring African countries.
articles.preview: Sudan Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighbouring African countries. Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.
articles.body:
Sudan

Tensions between Sudan and Ethiopia have escalated, with each accusing the other of supporting armed groups that wage war within its borders, undermining efforts to resolve the conflicts that have gripped the two neighbouring African countries.

Sudan’s military says Ethiopia has allowed Sudanese paramilitary forces battling the army to use its territory to set up camps, launch drones and stage cross-border attacks.

In early November, the Sudanese military filed complaints against Ethiopia with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, saying it submitted evidence to back up its case. Within days, Ethiopia expelled six staff members of a Sudanese Consulate and ordered the mission closed.

Ethiopia says the Sudanese military supports rebels fighting Ethiopian federal forces in its Tigray border region, where fighting returned in September, shattering a 2022 peace agreement.

Each country denies the other's accusations, and The Associated Press could not independently verify their claims. But the tensions — compounded by competing regional alliances and contentious issues over resources and disputed territory — risk a wider regional conflict.

Jervin Naidoo, a senior political economist at Oxford Economics Africa, told the AP that the situation “raises the risk that instability inside Ethiopia becomes another front in Sudan’s war — and vice versa.”

Here’s a closer look at what's behind the escalation and how it could impact the wider region:

Sudan’s military says Ethiopia backs Sudanese paramilitary forces

Sudan was plunged into war in April 2023, when long-simmering tensions between the army and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, turned into all-out fighting.

So far, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or ACLED, a conflict monitor, though aid groups warn that the real number is likely much higher. Some 13 million people have been displaced.

The war, now in its fourth year, has left the Sudanese military in control of the north, east and central regions, including Sudan’s Red Sea ports and its oil refineries and pipelines. The RSF and its allies control western Darfur and parts of Kordofan along the border with South Sudan — both regions rich in oil fields and gold mines.

The latest flashpoint in the war is in Sudan's Blue Nile province, which borders Ethiopia.

In late August, the Humanitarian Research Lab, a Yale University research group that uses satellite imagery to monitor conflicts, found an increase in military vehicles and equipment at an Ethiopian military base in Asosa, a city near the Sudanese border.

Based on satellite imagery, the Yale group confirmed the buildup was linked to the RSF.

“The RSF is engaged out of Ethiopia ... to try to open a second front,” said Nathaniel Raymond, head of the research group.

Ethiopia says Sudan’s military backs the Tigray rebels

Fighting resumed in September in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, where the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, and Ethiopian federal troops fought between 2020 and 2022, when a peace deal was signed.

Later that month, Ethiopia’s army chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, suggested that Sudan, Eritrea and Egypt were supporting rebel troops who at the time had captured several strategic towns. The allegations drew sharp denials from the three neighbours.

In early November, Ethiopia expelled the six staff members of Sudan’s mission in Asosa and closed the consulate.

Naidoo, from Oxford Economics Africa, warned that continued fighting in Tigray could divert Ethiopia’s attention from its myriad other issues and increase the risk of weapons and fighters flowing across the border with Sudan.

“All the ingredients are present for an intensifying proxy war between Ethiopia and Sudan that further destabilises both countries,” said Alan Boswell, Horn of Africa project director at the International Crisis Group.

Unresolved disputes, competing political alliances and a flashpoint border

Relations between Sudan and Ethiopia have deteriorated since late last year, when the RSF established camps on Ethiopian territory, according to Ladd Serwat, senior Africa analyst at ACLED.

In October, a drone strike blamed on the RSF hit a gathering of displaced people on Sudan's border with Ethiopia and killed 41, said the Emergency Lawyers rights group, which tracks the war in Sudan.

“Sudan and Ethiopia don’t operate in a vacuum; their relations amid these current domestic conflicts are shaped by external backers,” said Serwat, adding that Ethiopia is allied with the United Arab Emirates while Sudan is part of an Egypt-Eritrea regional alliance.

Turkey has been balancing, backing both Khartoum and Addis Ababa, he said.

Serwat added that Ethiopia’s support for the RSF is primarily logistical, while the UAE remains its main backer, funding camps and supplying weapons. The UAE has repeatedly denied any involvement in Sudan’s war.

Other issues have also marred relations, including Ethiopia's construction of a huge dam — Africa’s largest dam — on the Blue Nile, the main Nile River tributary. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam near the Ethiopia-Sudan border cost about $5 billion and was completed in 2025, aiming to boost Ethiopia's power production and economy.

But it has triggered a dispute with Egypt and Sudan, which have called for a legally binding agreement on the dam’s filling and operation to protect their own water resources.

Another issue is the disputed border region of Al-Fashaga, where Ethiopian farmers have long cultivated the area's fertile soil, according to the International Crisis Group. In late 2020, Sudanese troops moved in to reassert control over the area as Ethiopian troops were distracted fighting with the Tigray rebels.

The Sudan-Ethiopia tensions may not have gained much attention, but if ignored, they could escalate further and lead to mass displacements of people, Raymond's Yale group said.

articles.title: Peak Energy eyes South Korea green projects as war upends fuel flows
articles.summary: Peak Energy has $250 million in projects in South Korea and another $100 million's worth getting underway in 2027.
articles.preview: Countries including South Korea and the Philippines are becoming increasingly attractive to renewables developers such as Singapore-based Peak Energy, as governments accelerate clean energy adoption to overcome fuel disruptions due to the U.S.-Iran war. Seoul has “set targets to connect more power to the grid and push costs down,” said Gavin Adda, chief executive of the company backed by Stonepeak Partners, an alternative investment firm that manages about $98 billion in assets.
articles.body:
Countries including South Korea and the Philippines are becoming increasingly attractive to renewables developers such as Singapore-based Peak Energy, as governments accelerate clean energy adoption to overcome fuel disruptions due to the U.S.-Iran war.

Seoul has “set targets to connect more power to the grid and push costs down,” said Gavin Adda, chief executive of the company backed by Stonepeak Partners, an alternative investment firm that manages about $98 billion in assets. “You’re seeing a big increase in the number of developers trying to work out how to operate there.”

The growing interest comes as conflict in the Middle East continues to choke flows of liquefied natural gas from Qatar — the world’s second producer last year — and keeps prices of the fuel at multi-year highs. That’s forced governments to turn to alternatives, including accelerating the adoption of solar and wind. South Korea depended on Qatar for about 15% of its LNG supplies last year, according to World Bank data.

South Korean authorities in September announced measures to ease restrictions on renewable energy projects connecting to the power grid, particularly in the southwestern Honam region. The grid-connection date for one of Peak Energy’s solar farms has been brought forward by five years to 2029, with other developers seeing similar improvements, Adda said.

The country’s power demand should also increase as the artificial intelligence boom drives a rapid buildout of data centers, and Peak Energy has received requests to supply electricity to hyperscalers, he added.

Peak Energy has $250 million in projects in South Korea and another $100 million’s worth getting underway in 2027. These account for a large share of the firm’s 300 megawatts of operating assets, which are spread across eight Asia-Pacific markets including the Philippines, Japan, Australia and Taiwan.

The Iran conflict has also pushed the Philippines to bring renewable projects online earlier. The Southeast Asian country already allows full foreign ownership of projects and has a green lane to speed up approvals for major investments.

“It’s the fastest country in Asia for developing renewable projects,” Adda said in an interview last week. “So I can shake hands with you as a landowner, and I can start construction one year to 18 months later.”

The Philippines is expected to add 5.6 gigawatts of new solar capacity this year, more than all of its Southeast Asian peers, according to BloombergNEF forecasts. While the pipeline remains robust, the Department of Energy earlier this year terminated agreements for nearly 18 GW of clean-power projects, as many prospective investors had no plans to build them and were waiting to sell the rights.

articles.preview: In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
articles.body:
Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

Weekend roundup

- UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

- Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

- Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

- UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

- Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.

Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”

On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.

A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.

Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.

It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.

“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”

The week to come

- Tuesday | The former health and social care secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

- Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.

- Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

What else we’ve been reading

- With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

- Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy

- Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy

Sport

Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.

Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.

Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield

The front pages

“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.

The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.

Today in Focus

Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?

This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.

Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

Bored at work?

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.
